864.t: Having his own bass style that others cannot copy
864.s: Players try to copy his bass playing and fail; he insists every musician needs a style of his own.
864.ch: Style and old New Orleans customs
864.q: That's right. I make whatever comes in my mind to make it and ain't nobody else going to ever be a player. See, because when I find out they're playing the way they think they got it, I'll play it and put something else in.

198.t: Every clarinetist once had his own sound
198.s: Barnes says he wants to sound only like himself, and that today's players sound more alike.
198.q: You want to do like other guys do and let the whole lot know. I believe. I'm telling the truth in all my things. I'm joking. I don't care what to do, I don't like a none of man's style. I wouldn't want anybody to say that I sound like him. I sound like myself, do like myself. That's why you see I…

58.s: Miller says he was called the fast finger, did not learn it from anyone, and mentions his feature piece.
58.q: Well the show thing I used to call my feature.

900.t: Finding his own licks; Frank Rossolino and Matty Matlock's Abe Lincoln
900.s: He explains finding one's own sound rather than copying others, advising his son John.
900.q: It’s hard to say, it’s just little things that you do you know. Stuff that you heard or figured out. See there are guys that want to emulate a certain player. And I don’t want to mention any names but there are guys that can play exactly like somebody else. And I told my son when he started, now he…

535.t: Originators versus copycats; Billy Mitchell and Sweets Edison quotes
535.s: Responding to quotes from Mitchell and Edison, he talks about souls arriving with emotional baggage and how everyone borrows from predecessors before finding their own sound.
535.q: Billy Mitchell, sorry, yup. Billy Mitchell. The first thing I would say was that sometimes people when they come into this life they come in with heavy baggage. So they don’t even need to experience a lot of emotional stuff, they already have it, depending on their upbringing. They have their…

316.t: Imitation and finding your own style; Scott Hamilton
316.s: Young players shouldn't force uniqueness; Scott Hamilton evolved his own sound.
316.q: Well yeah, that’s probably right. I never thought of it that way. That’s right. That’s right. Well you don’t — I don’t think a young person should push themselves to become unique, you just let it happen. Maybe it will never happen I don’t know. But you know I’m thinking of Scott Hamilton. You know…

753.t: Armstrong's and Bix's limitations as part of their expression
753.s: Cullum argues that self-taught players' limitations shape their style and make them speak emotionally; he feels he knew Bix.
753.q: Well I think it’s a variety of things that create an emotional response. If you’ve got Armstrong, playing with a lot of passion and relatively few notes, and not unlimited technique. Now he could play anything he could think. But the whole system of his brain and his self-taught technique meant…

931.t: Influences: Parker, Pepper Adams' 'research' remark and Clark Terry
931.s: He tells of a saxophone clinic where Pepper Adams said copying one person is plagiarism but copying everybody is research; Rowe adds Clark Terry's imitation-assimilation-creation.
931.ch: Playing, influences and the Basie records
931.q: I guess, sure. I mean I was never good enough to copy anybody so I just probably — in the words of Pepper Adams, one time we were doing a clinic with the Thad Jones saxophone section. We had about 200 saxophone players in the room. So I said, “We

540.t: Finding your own sound instead of copying
540.s: Gardner agrees players today sound alike and says you must imitate first but then move beyond Freddie Hubbard and others to your own voice.
540.q: Well you know you have to sound like someone in order to sound like yourself. In the beginning of, in the formative years of your being able to play at an advanced skill level in improvisation, you’d want to sound like somebody else. Like Dizzy Gillespie sounded like Roy Eldridge in those early…

723.t: Learning by copying, then finding your own identity
723.s: Influence is fine but one should develop a personal sound, like learning to drive then driving your own way.
723.q: Yeah. Definitely. And another something too is now in order for me to learn how to drive a car, I have a take instructions from you and do what you do. But after I learn how to drive then I drive my own way. So that’s what they always said. You know you might have to copy somebody in order to learn…

161.t: Originality in jazz and copying like Sol Yaged
161.s: He admires Davern's creativity and says copying choruses is a fool's errand; one must be his own person.
161.q: More of a fire in him you know. And one of the reasons I like Kenny was you know Kenny didn’t particularly care for bebop. He made something out of traditional jazz. It became an individual thing, which I like, which I try to do, I’ve tried to do all my life. And strangely enough I think I’m coming…

414.s: Jimmy Zito's remark on jazz never being heard twice; Ross identifies Zito from Les Brown and the Tonight Show band.
414.q: Oh, yes. That’s the fun of it if you can. One friend of mine, Jimmy Zito, says the fun of jazz is that what you play at that particular time was never be heard before or be heard since. Some of it’s been heard before in my case.

582.t: Finding your own voice amid many influences
582.s: Nussbaum says he is a product of classical music, rock, Motown and Hendrix before jazz, and draws on many influences including non-musical ones.
582.q: I think that as time goes on we have to realize that nobody can be, like nobody can be me better than me. And I have to tap into all my different influences and I am my own person. And the way I look at things and the way that I am establishes and helps to shape what I’m about. I have a multitude…

216.t: Avoiding sounding the same: broad listening and Cannonball
216.s: Responding to Sweets Edison's remark, Ricker urges students to forge their own sound and listen widely; Rowe and Ricker name Cannonball and Getz.
216.q: Yeah, I think it’s something you can’t force you know. And you know if everybody is more or less doing, practicing the same stuff that’s going to — I mean you get out what’s put in and if you all are more or less inputting the same stuff through you, you know, the same play-a-long records, you…

757.t: Be yourself: the takeaway from interviews
757.s: Interviews with Miles, Rollins, Blakey and others taught him to be himself and stop comparing.
757.q: sound like somebody else you’re doomed to be second best, they’re already doing it. So at some point I really settled into owning my playing and not worrying about whether it was I don’t know, authentically part of the tradition or — I stopped comparing my performance and the time I put in and my…

141.s: Clyde Cox says he sounded like himself early; Allison says he just played as he thought he should.
141.q: I didn’t nurture it. I don’t think I was aware of it. I don’t know... But I just played the way I thought that I should play.

86.t: Be an originator, not an imitator
86.s: He advises youngsters not to copy Parker, Dizzy or Miles.
86.ch: Style, originality and the younger generation
86.q: No, whatever anybody’s doing that’s their thing, I’m not going to try….the old saying in New York used to be, they would rather be the world’s worst originator than to be the world’s greatest imitator. Which I agree with. Because if you’re an originator, I don’t care how bad it is, it’s your sound.…

371.t: Travel, culture and becoming the sum of one's experiences
371.s: Jones says a traveling musician absorbs languages and cultures and that his style is the sum of what he has absorbed, never copying note for note.
371.q: Well, I think that’s true, but that comes with the fact that the life that you live means that you have to travel a lot. You come into contact with a lot of different divergent cultures, and a lot of different languages. You may pick up a phrase here and you may pick up a phrase there. It gives you…

383.s: Wilson explains how Fats, Hines and Tatum were his idols and a player must eventually trust his own sound.
383.q: But eventually, it will come out -- the writing will come out pure, clear, loud and clean. If you just keep trying and don't back away from it, as over a period of time they will, so I think a young player, when they are developing an improvising style of your own. Because ideas do come to you, and…

413.t: Outgrowing your influences; knowing the heritage
413.s: A jazz player must stop copying and develop his own voice, but Hinton insists musicians know their heritage.
413.ch: Young players, schools and studio work
413.q: But see, I think also then when a black musician gets good and he gets his own style going, he becomes creative, he doesn't listen any more anyhow, because he's got his own thing going now, his own creativity and --
